tier_reason: Upgraded B to A: independent public harness (nordlow/compiler-benchmark cbench: bm_Rust, gcc_clang_op_flags, bm_C_and_Cxx_using_gcc/clang) fixes every flag (gcc/clang -Wall -Wextra at default -O0, rustc with no flags at opt-level 0), the README table names every compiler version, and the CPU is stated (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350, Arch Linux). All README numbers in the claim match the Rust, C and C++ rows.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 run, tables updated 2026-10-09), Total=Build+Run us/f (untemplated / templated): rustc 187 / 238 vs C gcc-15 392, C gcc-16 454, C++ g++-15 303 / 600, C++ g++-16 486 / 566, C++ clang++ 236 / 107, C clang 118. Derived from page data: 2.1x faster than gcc-15 and 2.4x faster than gcc-16 on C, 1.6x faster than g++-15 and 2.6x faster than g++-16 on untemplated C++, 2.5x faster than g++-15 and 2.4x faster than g++-16 templated, 1.26x faster than clang++ untemplated; 1.6x slower than clang C (118) and 2.2x slower than clang++ templated (107). The README highlight says 'rustc (187 µs/f) significantly outpaces GCC-based C/C++ (~450–486 µs/f)'; its Conclusions section, from an earlier run, says rustc (183 µs/f) 'handily outperforms both GCC-based C/C++ front-ends (~418–455 µs/f)'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Flags are in the public harness cbench (README's ./benchmark is a symlink to it; the same flag code is in benchmark at d16d0a5, the 2026-10-09 commit that updated the README tables): gcc/clang C build = -Wall -Wextra -o <exe> with no -O flag (GCC/Clang default -O0), C++ uses -Wno-c++11-extensions instead of the warning flags; rustc gets no flags (RUSTC_FLAGS = [], so opt-level 0 through LLVM with debug assertions and overflow checks on by default; the cranelift RUSTC_NIGHTLY_FLAGS list is defined but unused); zig build-exe -fno-llvm -fno-lld -fno-clang (Debug mode, Zig's self-hosted x86_64 backend and linker). Versions from the README table: rustc 1.100.0-nightly, zig 0.18.0-dev.35+5e754304d, gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1. Defaults: 200 chains x depth 200 = 40,000 functions per file, minimum of up to 10 builds (capped to 2-3 when a build exceeds 1-3 s), constants re-randomised per run to defeat caches.
corrections.caveats: Compile-time comparison of unoptimised builds on one synthetic translation unit of 40,000 arithmetic functions with no headers, standard library or module resolution (the README says it does not reflect real builds); not the wave's run-time -O3 comparison. The README does not state flags, but the harness does: gcc/clang get only -Wall -Wextra (default -O0) and rustc gets none (opt-level 0, debug assertions and overflow checks on), so optimisation levels are matched at 'unoptimised'. Not a language win: clang compiles the same C 1.6x faster than rustc (118 vs 187 us/f) and clang++ templated is 2.2x faster (107 vs 238); the margin over GCC comes from GCC's slower -O0 pipeline (gcc-16 compile-only 400 us/f against clang's 78) and a GCC 15 to 16 regression the README itself flags. The templated Rust source omits the per-function constants that the C++ templated source carries (cbench Rust leaf 'x', chain 'x + prev(x)'), so the 2.5x templated ratio compares slightly less code. One sample run with a large run-to-run spread: the README's Conclusions section (an earlier run) gives clang 87, rustc 183 and GCC 418-455 us/f, and in the table the gcc-15 C build (392) is twice its compile-only time (193.8) while the other GCC rows differ by 12-31%. Tasks run concurrently in a multiprocessing pool pinned to cores chosen by cpu_topology.py heuristics on a Zen 5/Zen 5c part, so rows may have run on different core types. GCC and clang skip some C++ semantic checks that rustc performs in full (README note). The sibling record for D (dmd) is from the same table. Independent suite, but a small one (167 stars), one machine.
corrections.why_faster: Compiler implementation, not language: cbench builds both sides unoptimised (gcc/clang default -O0, rustc opt-level 0 through LLVM), and the README attributes the GCC rows' cost to GCC's heavier backend (its dmd/ldmd2/gdc comparison is described as 'isolating backend cost'; gcc-16 compile-only is 400 us/f against clang's 78) plus a GCC 15 to 16 regression; clang, which shares rustc's LLVM backend, compiles the same C faster than rustc. The README also notes that GCC and clang skip some C++ semantic checks that rustc performs in full.

notes: Numbers and ratios check out against the README table; tier raised to A because the public harness pins every flag (no -O for gcc/clang/rustc) and the CPU and versions are stated. Shortcomings to record: compile-time of unoptimised builds on one synthetic file (off the wave's run-time -O3 baseline), rustc is slower than clang C (1.6x) and clang++ templated (2.2x) so the win is over GCC's backend, not a language effect; templated Rust source omits constants; single noisy run (README's own earlier run differs by up to 36% for clang).

tier_reason: First-party hyperfine screenshots (img/dev-random.png, test.mca.png, no-squeeze.bin.png, zeros.bin.png) show exactly the claimed means and ratios against system hexdump -C, with the hyperfine command in the README, but no CPU, OS, hexdump implementation/version or C build flags; the test files are generated locally and not published.

corrections.caveats: Different algorithm: system hexdump drives a generic format-string interpreter while src/main.rs hard-codes the one canonical layout with a hex lookup table and a BufWriter, so the 40x gap is a specialisation effect, not a language effect (inference; the README gives no mechanism). CPU, OS, hexdump implementation and version are not stated; hyperfine discards both tools' output; the numbers exist only as screenshots (which match the claimed figures), and the README text (14x, apparently from before the 2023-08-15 commit 'now ~40x speed difference') disagrees with the screenshots (up to 42x). The zeros.bin row (1.94x) is where both tools squeeze repeated lines. Output is not identical to hexdump -C: render_ascii prints '!' (0x21) and '~' (0x7e) as '.', a run of exactly one repeated line is dropped without the '*' marker, and -n/--length is ignored because end = (i + length).max(usize::MAX); the tests check helpers and two tiny inputs, never output against the real hexdump. These differences do not create a fast path (every line is still formatted), so the numbers stand. Tiny hobby repo (0 stars, 1 fork, 3 commits), last commit 2023-08-15.
corrections.why_faster: Specialisation, not language: src/main.rs formats each 16-byte line into a reused 79-byte Vec with a 16-entry hex lookup table and writes it through a BufWriter, whereas system hexdump interprets a generic format string per output unit (inference from the sources; the README names no mechanism).

notes: Screenshots confirm 42.00x, 38.62x, 37.86x and 1.94x; tier C stands. Shortcomings to record: specialised tool vs generic format interpreter (not a language effect), no hardware/hexdump version, README text says 14x vs 40x in description, output deviates from hexdump -C ('!' and '~' shown as '.', single repeated line dropped without '*', -n ignored), abandoned 0-star repo.
